Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years.

The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky.

Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA.

However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging.

Jupiter's Trojans are the most famous; the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center notes that an incredible 15,000 of these objects have been discovered so far. But some other planets, including Neptune, also host Trojans. In fact, a 2005 study suggested that Neptune has up to 10 times more Trojans than Jupiter. Until now, though, astronomers have spotted only 28 Neptunian Trojans, with just two of these being long-term L5 members.

There are two reasons why it's difficult to detect these rocks. First, the Neptunian Trojans are extremely faint. More critically, for nearly 15 years, the Trojan population's position in the sky relative to Earth has overlapped with the central region of the Milky Way. Consequently, bright background stars have made it nearly impossible to discern the tiny, faint asteroids, Megan Schwamb, the study's first author and a researcher who focuses on how planets and their building blocks form and evolve at Queen's University Belfast, told Live Science in an email.

An illustration of the Jovian Trojans orbiting in front of and behind Jupiter

However, from 2025 onward, the L5 group's position has moved — albeit extremely slowly — away from the galactic plane. This has made the population slightly easier to observe. At the same time, the Rubin Observatory started scanning the entire Southern Hemisphere sky with the world's largest digital camera.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Rubin is pretty uniquely suited to being excellent at discovering Neptune Trojans," study co-author Kathryn Volk, a scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, told Live Science in an email. "The on-sky density of these objects is not particularly high, so having a large field of view helps a lot!" (Rubin has a field of view equivalent to seven full moons, according to the observatory's website.) This, along with the observatory's excellent vision — which allows it to detect objects 100 billion times dimmer than Venus — enabled the discovery of the new Trojans.

The new Trojan observations form part of the Rubin Science Validation Survey, a three-month-long test run that was held in mid-2025 prior to the start of the observatory's flagship decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which is now underway. By chance, the Science Validation Survey encompassed the part of the sky containing Neptune's L5 Trojans, leading to the asteroids being photographed within three weeks of the survey's start.

Following the discoveries, the researchers created computer models to determine the asteroids' orbits. These simulations revealed that the duo will continue to tag behind Neptune for a billion years. The results suggest that the asteroids' trajectories have been stable for several billion years, which means the asteroids may have been traversing these routes from the time of the early solar system. The researchers also found a third object in Rubin's data, but it had a stable orbit in only some of their simulations, leading them to classify it as a candidate Trojan rather than a confirmed one.

However, the two confirmed Trojans likely didn't form in place alongside Neptune. The simulations showed that the asteroids' orbits are highly tilted, just like those of the previously discovered L5 asteroids — suggesting that Neptune captured these objects as they were hurtling past.

Determining the properties of both the Jovian and Neptunian Trojan asteroids will help researchers understand what happened during the solar system's infancy, when the giant planets are believed to have migrated to their present-day positions, Volk said.

Schwamb expects the LSST to unveil many more of the hypothesized Neptunian Trojans, especially because it will survey this same patch of the sky repeatedly over the next several months.

The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1010(2), L36. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aead9a

#6447. Scientists Discover an Ancient Herbal Remedy May Help Curb Binge Drinking

A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.

In a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo. The benefits persisted for three months after participants stopped taking the supplement.

The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a new strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.

Binge drinking accounts for more than half of the roughly 80,000 annual U.S. deaths attributed to excessive alcohol consumption. Despite the scale of the problem, fewer than 10% of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat the condition.

“Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” said Glenn-Milo Santos, PhD, MPH, the study’s lead author and a UCSF professor of community health systems. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit. What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day.”

The trial involved 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who engaged in binge drinking at least once a week. Binge drinking was defined as consuming at least five alcoholic drinks on a single occasion for men and at least four for women.

Participants were divided into two groups, with half receiving a standardized kudzu extract and the other half receiving a placebo. Over 12 weeks, they were instructed to take their assigned treatment approximately 2.5 hours before they anticipated drinking heavily. Everyone also received brief weekly counseling sessions.

By the end of the trial, participants taking kudzu had reduced their average number of binge-drinking days from 2.15 to 1.42 per week. Those receiving the placebo showed little improvement, with their weekly average declining from 2.15 to 2.06 days.

Kudzu also reduced how frequently participants experienced weeks involving any binge drinking. The proportion of such weeks dropped from 88% to 58% among those taking the extract, compared with a decline from 88% to 81% in the placebo group.

Three months after the treatment period ended, participants who had received kudzu continued to report significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those in the placebo group. Researchers suggest that drinking less during the trial may have helped participants reconsider their drinking habits and develop greater confidence in their ability to control their alcohol consumption.

Participants tolerated the kudzu extract well, experiencing no more side effects than those receiving the placebo. No serious adverse effects were linked to the treatment.

However, the researchers caution against assuming that commercially available kudzu supplements will deliver comparable benefits. The trial used a standardized formulation, whereas the composition of products sold over the counter can vary considerably. Larger clinical studies are needed to confirm the results across more diverse populations.

Reference: “Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial” by Glenn-Milo Santos, Phillip Coffin, Allie Dunham, Thomas Hoffmann, John Walker, Tim Matheson and Steven Batki, 3 November 2026, American Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1176/appi.ajp.20251354

This study was funded by National Institutes for Health (R01AA025930). Santos is also supported by a K24 career development grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), which is part of the NIH.

#6446. The Maya People Loved the Color Red. Scientists Say It May Have Helped Bring Them Down.

The reddish pigment cinnabar was so popular that it seeped into the water supply around Maya settlements, setting off a disastrous downstream effect.

The Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The new analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he said. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”

The source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters said. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters said. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

#6445. Why Mega-Constellations Have a Hidden Space Junk Blind Spot

We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is âsafeâ in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

To understand why, letâs look at how engineers currently grade collision risk. Standards set by NASA and the European Space Agency rely on color-coded charts that sort missions into one of several buckets based on their risk profile. Categories like âLow,â âMedium,â and âHighâ are self-explanatory, but they eliminate important distinctions in risk profiles, and only look at one satellite at a time. And, crucially, they focus solely on the risk to the company that launched them.

If a company funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company. But if a mega-constellation operator builds thousands of identical satellites at a cost of a million dollars a pop, losing one barely registers on their financial statements. Consequently, according to the risk profile, all relatively inexpensive, reproducible satellites that make up the mega-constellations end up with a âLowâ risk profile.

Fraser talks about how we make sure satellites don't crash into each other.

The algorithm described in the paper exposes the flaw in that logic by separating the risk into two different scores. First is the âIndividual Riskâ â i.e. the traditional metric of the financial hit a satelliteâs owner takes if the spacecraft is destroyed by collision. The second is the âCollective Riskâ, which ignores the cost of each individual satellite, but captures the physical danger each imposes on every other operational satellite in its altitude band across its entire operational and disposal lifetime.

Mathematically, this is a way of capturing the âtragedy of the commonsâ aspect of orbital space. Economists have long warned that when a âpublic goodâ (such as an orbital path) is free to use, users, whether they are farmers on a field or launch companies trying to build internet satellite constellations, have an incentive to utilize as much of the free resource as they can while not paying any attention to the consequences of that use.

In orbit, those consequences take the form of congestion, dodging maneuvers, and potential destruction of other satellites that are forced on every other company if one decides to ignore their responsibility to properly manage the impact their equipment has on an orbit. As weâve reported before, those consequences are growing, with an average Starlink satellite having to fire its thruster at least once a week to dodge a potential collision.

Fraser talks about how space junk could eventually block our access to orbit.

Starlink itself is a good case in point. A single Starlink V2 Mini, orbiting at 525 km, has a collective risk 317 times higher than the âindividual risk.â In a traditional risk assessment, this would mark it as âLowâ risk, whereas this new framework would place it very clearly in the âVery Highâ camp.

There have been some efforts to capture this long-term environmental impact already. ESA uses an index called the Environmental Consequences of Orbital Breakups (ECOB) and researchers at EPFL in Switzerland have put forward the Space Sustainability Rating. However, the simulations underpinning these metrics are computationally expensive and require hours to complete. The tool Toson developed in MATLAB runs in seconds on a standard computer and matches the higher-end benchmarks exceptionally well.

Itâs all good to simply update the categorization of a satellite for its collective risk, but having that information is useless if operators and regulators donât do anything with it. Toson suggests updating the international debris guidelines and licensing rules to take this new metric into account. If a company wants to launch a low-cost satellite that will affect the orbital environment for everyone else, they should be required to either fund active debris cleanup or accept a cap on the total risk posed by their fleet of spacecraft.

Fraser talks about real-life advanced tech that can remove space debris.

Regulators havenât had much time to digest this new idea, so donât expect to see any such rules anytime soon. But as our orbital highways become more and more congested, satellite operators will need more guidance on how to maintain the commons before we end up in a Kessler Syndrome situation. This new paper may contribute to that standards-setting â and the sooner the better.

F. Toson - A simplified engineering algorithm for collision risk assessment and classification of LEO satellites

UT - Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting TrashâItâs About Control and Economics

UT - Are Mega-Constellations Sleepwalking Low Earth Orbit into Runaway Chaos?

#6444. A Newly Discovered Group of Immune Cells May Be Working Against You

Researchers have identified a previously unknown group of aging immune cells that may undermine the body’s natural defenses.

Some aging immune cells do more than lose their ability to fight disease. Researchers at Monash University have identified a previously unknown group of immune cells that actively suppress the body’s defenses, potentially helping explain why cancer and serious infections become more common with age.

The discovery comes from a preclinical study published in Science Immunology. Using mouse models, scientists mapped genetic changes that cause immune cells to deteriorate in different ways, identifying potential targets for treatments aimed at preserving immune function later in life.

The researchers investigated CD8+ T cells, immune cells responsible for recognizing and destroying infected and cancerous cells. They identified three distinct ways aging disrupts the genetic programs controlling these cells, impairing their ability to respond to unfamiliar threats, regulate immune activity, and maintain normal cellular health.

“Aging is the biggest risk factor for cancer overall,” said Dr. Daniel Thiele, the study’s first author at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute. “Our immune system is constantly surveying our bodies for potentially cancerous cells and eliminating them, often without us ever knowing.”

“As we age, this natural defense system becomes less effective, making us more vulnerable to cancer and infections and reducing our ability to respond to vaccines.”

“This study provides a blueprint of immune aging, from which we can now identify potential targets to reverse aspects of that decline.”

The findings challenge the idea that immune cells simply become progressively weaker as they age. Some lose their protective functions, while others develop the ability to interfere with neighboring immune cells. These different patterns can occur within the same aging individual.

“Even within the same aging individual, we found that immune cells can age in remarkably different ways,” Dr. Thiele said. “Some cells lose their ability to protect us against disease, while others begin to interfere with the body’s own immune defenses.”

“By understanding what goes wrong within these cells, we can begin to identify more targeted ways to restore immune function as we age.”

The research has also contributed to a separate discovery involving granzyme K, a protein produced by immune cells. In that study, Monash scientists identified granzyme K as a driver of age-related organ damage in mice, suggesting that changes in immune cell behavior may affect tissues beyond the immune system itself.

The findings raise the possibility of developing therapies that address specific mechanisms of immune aging rather than attempting to stimulate the entire immune system. Such treatments remain a future prospect, with the current evidence coming from preclinical research.

“By understanding what drives aging within our immune cells, we may ultimately be able to target not only immune aging, but aging throughout the body,” said Professor Nicole La Gruta, the study’s senior researcher at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.

Reference: “Aging drives distinct chromatin signatures of CD8 T cell dysfunction and the emergence of a unique CD8 Treg cell population” by Daniel Thiele, Liam C. Kealy, David Chisanga, Brendan E. Russ, Angela Nguyen, Jessica Runting, Iona S. Schuster, Adele Barugahare, Tabinda Hussain, Mohammad Asadian, Minh Bui, Taylah J. Bennett, Nemo Shindo, Justin B. Zhang, Jasmine Li, Mariapia A. Degli-Esposti, Axel Kallies, Kim Good-Jacobson, Colby Zaph, Stephen J. Turner and Nicole L. La Gruta, 20 November 2026, Science Immunology. DOI: 10.1126/sciimmunol.aej5412

#6442. A Dark Energy Camera Portrait of the Betta Fish Nebula

This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

Astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

One of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

Only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

This close-up view shows one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License

What's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'

This is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It shows what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024)

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

These images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

This zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. #6441. The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

The Government Accountability Office secretly tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok and found that all four would help make plans when prompted.

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a new tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a press statement. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh said in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6440. “This Star System Should Not Exist”: Astronomers Discover a Cosmic Mystery Just 28 Light-Years Away

A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.

A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble. Astronomers looking for planets around a dim red star 28 light-years from Earth measured a wobble more than a thousand times larger than they expected. Following that motion revealed a family of three stars, two of which had already run out of fuel.

“We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”

The star they were watching was a red dwarf, a star much dimmer than the Sun. At the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, a planet-hunting instrument called SPIRou (SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge) picked up a change of nearly 16 kilometers (10 miles) per second in the star’s speed. After several years of follow-up observations, the team knew that whatever was tugging on the red dwarf had more than half the Sun’s mass.

“The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star,” said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and co-author of the study. “The most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldn’t be ruled out.”

The team finally saw the faint companion with Gemini North, another telescope on Maunakea. High-resolution images from its ʻAlopeke instrument showed a white dwarf orbiting the red dwarf. A white dwarf is the extremely dense core a star leaves behind after it runs out of fuel. Most stars, including the Sun, will end their lives this way.

Astronomers already knew about a white dwarf much farther out. That outer star circles both the red dwarf and its newly spotted companion. No other trio like this one, named Welopōʻai, is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

Before it became a white dwarf, the red dwarf’s closer neighbor was about 40 percent more massive than the Sun. As it aged, it swelled into a giant several hundred times its original size. The red dwarf would have been close enough for the expanding giant to affect it. In similar systems, a giant can swallow its companion, and the two stars can even merge. Welopōʻai’s red dwarf appears to have survived. It now circles the remnant in a stable orbit, farther away than astronomers would expect given how close the two once were.

“This system should not exist,” said Patrick Dufour, a professor at Université de Montréal who studies white dwarfs and co-authored the paper. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

The team wants to find out whether the pull of all three stars on one another could explain the inner pair’s orbit. The researchers also measured the inner white dwarf’s mass with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent. Astronomers rarely get such a precise mass for a white dwarf, and it gives them a way to test predictions about how stars age and how matter behaves when packed so tightly together. The international team, led by IREx, reported its in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The simulation illustrates how gravitational interactions between its three stars could influence their orbits over time. The sonification translates the stars’ orbital motions into sound, so you can hear the system’s changing rhythms. Credit: Heidi White (UMONTREAL/IREx). Simulation data: Alexandre Correia, University of Coimbra

Welopōʻai got its name through A Hua He Inoa (“To Call Forth a Name”), a program of the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The name joins welo, an inherited or family trait, with pōʻai, an orbit or circular path. Together they evoke a “path of family traits.”

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” Artigau said. “Even when we’re searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.”

Reference: “Welopō‘ai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun” by Étienne Artigau, Charles-Antoine Parent, Atanas K. Stefanov, Érika Le Bourdais, Souleymane Ouedraogo, Alexandrine L’Heureux, Patrick Dufour, René Doyon, Neil J. Cook, Charles Cadieux, Clémence Fontanive, Luc Arnold, Jean-François Donati, Matthias R. Schreiber, Ryan Cloutier, Xavier Delfosse, Céline Reylé, Thierry Forveille, Tianqi Cang, Claire Moutou and Alexandre C. M. Correia, 19 November 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202661214

#6439. The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

It's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's plans to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

On top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?"

This is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts."

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the issue:

When we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

While analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively new idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA)

Since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:

While extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

The second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:

No matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund

The second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate."

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she said. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next."

Lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:

From Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

Mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the issue was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:

Further Reading: Astrosociological Insights Forum, vol. 10, issue 1

#6438. Scientists Discover That Jupiter and Dead Stars Could Hold Clues to Dark Matter’s Biggest Mystery

The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering new clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen. Known as dark matter, it is thought to make up about 85% of all matter, yet its true nature remains a mystery. Researchers know it exists largely because of its gravitational effects, but they still do not know what it is made of.

Scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any. One possibility is that some particles move so slowly that they barely register in laboratory experiments. However, those same particles might be easier to find in places much larger than any detector on Earth: planets and stars.

Researchers Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard, and Gaurav Tomar investigated whether these celestial bodies could act as natural traps for dark matter. Their study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), found no evidence of dark matter but helped rule out certain possibilities about its properties.

Dark matter is known to interact through gravity, but scientists suspect it may also have extremely weak electrical or magnetic properties. Some particles could carry a tiny electric charge or behave like miniature magnets, allowing them to interact with ordinary matter in ways that are difficult to detect.

Speed could make those interactions even harder to observe. When a slow-moving particle strikes material inside a detector, it may transfer too little energy to produce a measurable signal. Inside a planet or star, however, even a small loss of energy could be enough to prevent the particle from escaping the object’s gravitational pull.

Over billions of years, these trapped particles could accumulate near the center of a planet or star. If their properties allow it, they might eventually collide and undergo a process called annihilation, transforming into other particles. Some of the resulting particles could escape into space, while others could release energy that warms the surrounding material.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” explains Gaurav Tomar, a researcher at the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea and the study’s corresponding author. “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”

The researchers used two different approaches to look for signs of dark matter. For Earth and the Sun, they examined existing searches for neutrinos, tiny particles that can travel through enormous amounts of matter without being stopped. If dark matter particles were annihilating deep inside these bodies, some of the resulting neutrinos might reach detectors and provide evidence of what was happening.

For Jupiter and white dwarfs, which are dense remnants of stars, the team looked at heat instead. Unlike the Sun, these objects are not powered by ongoing nuclear fusion, making them potentially useful places to investigate whether another source of energy is contributing to their warmth.

The researchers calculated how much heat different types of dark matter could produce if captured inside these objects, then compared those predictions with the energy the objects actually emit. If a particular type of dark matter would generate more heat than an object releases, that scenario could be ruled out.

By combining these calculations with existing observations, the team excluded several combinations of dark matter particle mass and electromagnetic properties that previous experiments had not eliminated. Earth was particularly useful for investigating particles with extremely small electric charges, while white dwarfs helped constrain other possible electromagnetic interactions.

The findings also come with an important uncertainty. How much dark matter a celestial body could capture depends partly on how much dark matter surrounds it. For white dwarfs in particular, researchers must rely on estimates because the local dark matter density is not always known.

“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar notes.

He was referring to the M4 star cluster, where the white dwarfs examined in the study are located. The amount of dark matter in that region has not been directly measured and must instead be estimated using models.

Looking ahead, Tomar suggests searching for even colder white dwarfs in regions thought to contain more dark matter. Because these stars emit relatively little heat, any additional warming from trapped particles could be easier to identify. Planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system could also offer new opportunities to investigate whether dark matter is quietly accumulating inside celestial bodies.

Reference: “Celestial probes of dark matter electromagnetic interactions” by Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard and Gaurav Tomar, August 27, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2608.27957

A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease.

The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes.

Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" cells would.

To flip that switch in the cells, a molecule latches onto the spool that DNA is wound around, specifically near genes involved in sparking inflammation. That subtle molecular tweak "holds those genes poised for rapid activation," said Musa Mhlanga, a cell biologist and molecular geneticist at the Radboud Institute for Molecular Life Sciences in the Netherlands who wasn't involved in the new study.

However, scientists didn't know how that change was maintained over time.

The immune memory should have been destroyed soon after it was made, given that "the cell has enzymes whose entire job is to strip that mark off," Mhlanga told Live Science in an email. But somehow, the memory stuck. "So the obvious question was never really answered: how does a mark survive weeks or months against machinery actively removing it?" Mhlanga said.

The research focused on cells of the innate immune system, including macrophages (pictured), which gobble up germs, dead cells and cellular debris.

The new study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Science Immunology, may answer that question.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The research investigated the phenomenon in mouse immune cells and live lab mice, as well as some human cells in lab dishes. Past studies hinted that, when immune cells switch into their "primed" state, their metabolism changes. This, in turn, drives up the production of a molecule called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which has long been known to help regulate how DNA gets packaged in cells.

In this case, though, the molecule took on a surprising role, Mhlanga said. NAD+ usually gets used up when enzymes orchestrate chemical reactions. But when it comes to the enzymes that normally erase immune cells' memory, called KDM5a, that wasn't the case.

NAD+ latches onto that epigenetic eraser but doesn't get used up in the process; instead, it shuts down KDM5a, as if it were pushing an "off" button. By restraining its memory eraser, the immune cell remains in a primed and activated state, ready to ignite inflammation when triggered.

In experiments with mice, the researchers found that reducing or eliminating NAD+ from immune cells prevented them from entering this primed state. In mice with cancer, this hobbled the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells.

Additionally, in aging mice, the team observed that NAD+ levels dwindle in concert with the innate immune system's ability to respond to threats. The research builds a convincing "molecular bridge" between those two facts, Mhlanga said, raising a hypothesis for why immunity gets worse with age.

Broadly, the research adds to scientists' understanding of how innate immune cells enter this primed, inflammatory state. This line of research may help scientists understand "why some vaccines protect against diseases they were never designed for," Mhlanga said.

For example, a tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BDG) is thought to mount a broad immune response that may help stave off many conditions, from viral infections to Alzheimer's disease. (Some scientists think that Alzheimer's stems from a dysregulated immune response that BCG may help to normalize.)

While this line of research could have wide-ranging applications, the new study has some limitations. The researchers did a few experiments with human cells and backed up some of their findings in mice with data from human cancer patients. However, "the human data are thin by comparison with the mouse work," Mhlanga noted, so they bear further confirmation.

In the future, he'd be interested in studies exploring NAD+ in the context of the aging immune system, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The recent research hints that pushing NAD+ to optimal levels could help counter each of these conditions.

But especially in cancer, where the disease's biology varies by the tumour type and stage, "it is not a simple 'more NAD+ is better' story," he cautioned, "and I'd resist it being written as one."

#6436. A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

Highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe."

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," said study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," said Vlemmings.

This figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

For now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

The flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a new element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â said Andriantsaralaza.

This research shows that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

"The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," said Vlemmings.

#6435. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6434. This Company Wants to Make Fuel From Carbon Dioxide—Using the Power of a Nuclear Reactor

AIRCO hopes to make a carbon-neutral fuel from captured CO2 and hydrogen. Some sustainability experts are skeptical.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry shows no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the company’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— new fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6433. NASA-Funded Study Reveals a Hidden Effect of Space Radiation on the Brain

New NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.

Cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear. A new NASA-funded study in mice found distinct molecular responses to simulated space radiation, raising questions about how prolonged exposure could affect astronauts traveling to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space. These highly energetic particles, often described as cosmic “rays,” can damage spacecraft electronics and potentially affect living tissue. Understanding their effects on the brain is a major concern for future missions beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field.

Researchers at the University of Rochester exposed male and female mice to simulated galactic cosmic radiation at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Led by neuroscience graduate student Mark Osabutey, MBChB, the team used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine nearly 16,000 microglia, the brain’s resident immune cells. This technique allowed scientists to investigate how radiation affected gene activity in individual cells.

The analysis, published in Scientific Reports, identified different molecular responses in males and females. Male microglia showed changes involving cellular stress adaptation and metabolism, while female microglia exhibited broader reductions in immune signaling pathways. Neither group showed widespread inflammatory activation or detectable radiation-related cognitive or behavioral impairment at the time of testing.

“Surprisingly, despite clear molecular changes, we found no widespread inflammatory activation or measurable radiation-associated behavioral impairment at the time we examined,” said Osabutey. The findings suggest that cellular responses to radiation can occur without immediately producing measurable functional problems, although their longer-term effects remain unknown.

Despite these sex-specific differences, researchers identified one response shared by both groups. Levels of FKBP5, a protein involved in regulating cellular stress responses, increased in the cortex and dentate gyrus of male and female mice. These brain regions contribute to functions including cognition, learning, and memory.

“We now need to understand whether FKBP5 plays a protective or harmful role, and how different radiation exposures and other spaceflight stressors influence long-term brain health,” said Osabutey. “Our findings highlight the importance of considering biological sex when assessing neurological risks during spaceflight and identify potential pathways for developing protective strategies.”

University of Rochester Professor of Neuroscience M. Kerry O’Banion, MD, PhD, has investigated the neurological effects of space radiation for more than 15 years. A member of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience, O’Banion previously contributed to research indicating that cosmic radiation could accelerate the onset of Alzheimer’s disease.

“We know cognitive changes from exposure to radiation in space are a real risk,” O’Banion said. “It’s important we understand how brain cells are changed. Knowing which mechanisms are impacted and how may help the development of countermeasures to protect or lessen an astronaut’s exposure to space radiation.”

The latest findings do not establish whether the observed immune cell changes are harmful, protective, or temporary. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether they contribute to neurological problems after prolonged exposure. “Additional studies examining other time points and effects in other experimental systems will be required to understand this further,” O’Banion said.

Osabutey has participated in NASA-funded research since joining O’Banion’s laboratory. In 2023, he received a NASA predoctoral grant augmentation award to investigate changes in microglial populations following exposure to galactic cosmic radiation. He has also presented the laboratory’s research at a NASA conference and attended the European Space Agency Summer School in Darmstadt, Germany.

“Receiving NASA support has allowed me to contribute to research addressing questions of national and international importance,” said Osabutey. “As a physician-scientist in training, I could not have asked for a better environment in which to train, and the experience has taught me how to pursue meaningful scientific questions through rigorous basic/translational investigation and collaboration, skills that I will carry forward in my future efforts to better understand brain injury and neurological disease.”

The research involved a broader collaboration between University of Rochester scientists and personnel at Brookhaven National Laboratory, where particle accelerators generate radiation conditions relevant to spaceflight.

“Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows have been an essential part of our NASA research effort,” O’Banion said. “It’s comprised of a large team that includes the outstanding organizational skills of our long-time senior research technician, Lee Trojanczyk, as well as support personnel at Brookhaven National Labs. Over time, nearly a dozen University of Rochester trainees have contributed to this work.”

Reference: “Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals sex-specific microglial responses to simulated galactic cosmic radiation without broad inflammatory activation” by Mark A. Osabutey, Lia Calcines-Rodríguez, Lee A. Trojanczyk, John A. Olschowka and M. Kerry O’Banion, 20 November 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-77661-9

This research was supported by a NASA grant and a NASA Human Research Program Grant Augmentation Award.
