In the wake of Elie's new findings, Live Science asked its readers what animal they would want to talk to if they could.

Over 550 people voted in our poll, with 54% picking dog. The next-largest voting group, 28% of respondents, chose cat.

The comments reflected the obvious trend of readers wanting to speak to their pets. One commenter wrote, "Cats, simply because I've had more of them as pets over the decades than anything else. I don't think spiders would be interesting conversationalists, I'm unlikely to encounter whales here in the middle of North America, and dogs that I meet on my daily walks are only invested in the canine treats I carry."

Another reader said we'd never be able to understand our pets even if we could communicate with them. "Unfortunately you would have to experience the world through your nose to truly understand what they experience. To understand what a dog is thinking you would have to 'be' a dog. A problem with communicating with any non-human being, whether it be octopi, whale, cat or extra terrestrial. It seems to be a human thing that people can't just sit, observe and interpret the world around them as it is. Everything needs to be explained!"

Not everyone chose cats and dogs, though. One reader wrote, "I would want to know my horse's backstory."

Several other commenters mentioned octopuses, with one commenter saying, "I’m disappointed that octopi weren't included on the list. I've read that they are incredibly intelligent, interact with humans and are able to think and plan. Also they can shape shift and change color and patterns. I love my dogs but I don't imagine they are capable of matching the observations and conversations octopi might have."

#6416. ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula. Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled "The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530â0213." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530â0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ringâfirst evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon starâand a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

âMost of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a starâs death throes,â said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. âItâs the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.â

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530âs central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

âDying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,â said Sahai. âIRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation weâve been using.â

IRAS 06530 also has a chemical composition that's challenging to understand. It's significantly enriched in 13C, 17O, and modestly enriched in 15N.

"Compared with solar values, the torus of IRAS 06530 appears to be significantly (modestly) enriched in 13C and 17O (15N), as wellâa pattern of rare-isotope enrichment inconsistent with standard nucleosynthesis models," the authors write.

Â¹Â³C and Â¹â·O are expected, but Â¹âµN isn't. It should be destroyed and depleted to solar levels. Again, a binary companion could be one explanation for this anomaly, and future observations might find one. It's also possible that atypical bursts of nuclear burning are responsible, but that's beyond the scope of this work.

Finding the first direct evidence of a dying star's thermal pulse, something indicated by theory, is the kind of progress astrophysicists hope to make.

âItâs essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, weâve mostly inferred from theoretical models,â said Sahai. âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â

#6415. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123

“The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene.”

The article doesn’t really support their claim of “increasing synchrony.” This sounds more like assigning a scapegoat than explaining what is driving the alleged changes. It appears to me that the relationship is best described by a U-shaped function rather than a linear, long-term trend. The index graph that is most U-like is the one going back farthest in time, suggesting some periodicity related to time.

The R^2 value in all cases is less than 0.5, and in most cases less than 0.2. That means that the variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the changes in the independent variable is less than the probability of getting a ‘Head’ in a coin flip. That doesn’t convince me that they really understand what is going on. But the buzzword salad had all the right words and conclusions to get published!

#6413. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability

#6412. Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang says.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017

#6411. The Event Horizon Telescope Views the Dynamics and Geometry of a Black Hole Jet in Extreme Detail

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jet emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at sub-parsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers - Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) - that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, the jet coming from its center is powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

An image of the core region of Messier 87, a supermassive black hole, processed from an array of radio telescopes known as the EHT with colours indicating brightness temperature (Credit: Event Horizon Telescope)

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik MÃ¼ller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut fÃ¼r Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alpes to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain. They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine, and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019. As MÃ¼ller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software were used during early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

Illustration of the multiwavelength 3C 279 jet structure in April 2017. The observing epochs, arrays, and wavelengths are noted in each panel. Credit: J.Y. Kim/MPIfR/VLBA and GMVA/EHT

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented towards our instruments, MÃ¼ller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending towards Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said MÃ¼ller:

We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.

While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen. Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images on how it behaves at the sub-parsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said MÃ¼ller:

This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.

We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.

#6410. Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, said the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West said.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”

The researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532

In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6408. Study Finds Artemis Astronauts Will Enjoy Moon-Grown Potatoes

By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©. Nevertheless, one can't help but recall the scene whenever news breaks about the latest experiment that examines the potential of growing plants in extraterrestrial soils. The latest comes from Oregon State University (OSU), where researchers have shown that potatoes grown in lunar soil simulant (amended with organic matter) are safe to eat and grow just as well as those produced on Earth.

This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay. Through the Artemis Program, crews will land around the South Pole-Aitken Basin and begin constructing a permanent base that will enable regular missions in the future (about one per year). China's National Space Agency (CNSA) and Roscosmos also plan on building a base - the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) - in the same region by the end of the decade.

To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required. Whereas the International Space Station (ISS) is resupplied regularly and emergency supplies can be dispatched within hours, missions to the Moon will take at least three days to arrive. As such, any sustained program of exploration on the Moon must rely on In-Situ Resource Utilization(ISRU) as much as possible - i.e., using local resources for building materials and providing astronauts with water and food.

Research in the past few decades has led to methods for 3D printing habitats and other facilities using lunar regolith. This can be combined with a bonding agent to create "lunacrete," or sintered with microwaves to create molten ceramic. Either material is then deposited layer by layer by construction robots to form walls and other structural elements. While hydroponics remain a viable way to grow plants (as astronauts do aboard the ISS), the real question is whether Earth plants can be grown in lunar regolith and other extraterrestrial soils.

Led by Aymeric Goyer, a professor with OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, the Oregon team used lunar regolith simulants with different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich organic soil produced when earthworms break down organic matter. With support from NASA's Johnson Space Center Simulant Development Lab, the team produced healthy potatoes with yields comparable to crops grown by farmers in Oregon (the 4th largest potato producer in the U.S.).

Goyer and his teams specifically selected potatoes because they produce more calories per square meter of soil than many other crops. They also offer substantial nutritional value: one medium skin-on potato (148 g/5.3 oz) provides roughly 110 calories, 26 g of carbohydrates, 3 g of protein, and 2 g of fiber. They are also naturally fat-free, gluten-free, cholesterol-free, and are therefore considered a practical staple food for long-duration space missions.

Since lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the researchers tested five simulants representing lunar mare (fine-grained basaltic soil) and lunar highland (feldspar-rich volcanic soil) regions. They also included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which produces the world's highest potato yield. The results showed that potato plants grown in simulants containing 30% vermicompost grew as well as those cultivated in Earth soils. In other samples, plants grown without vermicompost were severely stunted and had underdeveloped root systems.

The "Moon Village" concept, conceived by MIT in collaboration with the ESA and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Credit: ESA/Skidmore, Owings & Merrill

Lastly, those grown with 5% to 15% vermicompost showed only partial growth. As Goyer said in an OSU press release:

We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.

The results also showed that the potatoes grown in lunar regolith simulants maintained their nutritional quality, with no statistically significant increase in naturally occurring potato toxins (glycoalkaloids) often associated with green discoloration. Lunar regolith still presents many challenges for plant growth, which include extremely fine-grained dust and elevated levels of heavy metals.

But the researchers are confident that adding organic matter helps bind heavy metals, preventing them from damaging roots, interfering with growth, or leaching into the potatoes themselves. In the future, astronauts could bring compost to the Moon, along with Earth worms, to create their own fertilizer, augmenting soil collected during surface trips to grow their food.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab. Their results are reported in a paper, "Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants," that appeared in npj Microgravity. Another paper, which reports the results of experiments involving 10 potato varieties to identify which grow best in lunar soil, will be released.

#6407. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6406. Intermittent Fasting May Not Work the Way Scientists Thought for Liver Health

A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A new clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

The researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine. That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6.6 to 8.8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

Participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), late eating (2 p.m. to 10 p.m.), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p.m. to 8 p.m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

Although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.

For the researchers, “the most important factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”

References: “Time-restricted eating, liver health, and fecal microbiota in adults with overweight or obesity: A randomized controlled trial” by Manuel Dote-Montero, Antonio Clavero-Jimeno, Adrián Cortés-Martín, Amaya Lopez-Pascual, Elisa Merchán-Ramírez, Alba Camacho-Cardenosa, Mara Concepción, Maddi Osés, Alejandro López-Vázquez, Francisco J Amaro-Gahete, Juan J Martin-Olmedo, Lucas Jurado-Fasoli, Alejandro De-la-O, Patricia V García Pérez, Julio Gálvez, Alba Rodriguez-Nogales, Federico Garcia, Carmen Mbongo Habimana, Marcos Jiménez Vázquez, Víctor Manuel Alfaro-Magallanes, Matías A Avila, Jose L Martín-Rodríguez, Rafael Cabeza, Manuel Muñoz-Torres, Idoia Labayen and Jonatan R Ruiz, 7 July 2026, JHEP Reports. #6405. Euclid's Record-Setting Quasar Probes Black Hole Formation

Quasars are the cosmos' most luminous objects, generated by supermassive black holes (SMBH) that are accreting enormous amounts of matter. Astronomers keep finding these massive objects further and further back in time. The ESA's Euclid just found the newest record holder: the telescope observed it 40 million years sooner than the previous record-holder, and it was found at redshift z=8.13, corresponding to about 630 million years after the Big Bang. That's firmly in the Epoch of Reionization.

The quasar's technical name is J1504+6252, but it's been given the more recognizable name DÃºn Aonghasa. DÃºn Aonghasa is an ancient stone fort on top of a cliff in Ireland, where it looks out over the Atlantic Ocean.

The discovery is in research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole." The lead author is Julien Wolf, who was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy when the research was done.

One of the hallmarks of modern astronomy is the discovery of massive objects in the Universe that formed much sooner than astronomers thought they could. The JWST is driving much of this.

"Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history," the authors write.

Now the Euclid Space Telescope is contributing to that trend. Euclid was launched to study dark energy and the expansion of the Universe. A big part of that job is measuring galaxies at different redshifts in its Euclid Wide Survey, to see how their morphologies are different over time. That will reveal how dark energy has changed over time.

This is what DÃºn Aonghasa, the new quasar, looks like in the actual Euclid image. It's the red dot in the center. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/J. Wolf et al.

Euclid found DÃºn Aonghasa in its Euclid Wide Survey imaging, but didn't confirm it. Follow-up observations by Keck, the Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope, and especially the JWST provided the confirmation. JWST spectroscopy let the researchers measure "a systemic redshift of zsysâ=â8.129âÂ±â0.005, corresponding to only 630âMyr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by â39âMyr," the authors write. 39 million years is about 6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch. The quasar is now the first quasar observed at z > 8.

DÃºn Aonghasa's luminosity is what lets astronomers observe it at such a great distance. Its luminosity helped researchers measure its mass and its accretion rate, and DÃºn Aonghasa contains 360 million solar masses.

This figure shows absolute UV magnitude as a function of redshift for high-redshift quasars, galaxies, LRDs, LBDs, and other JWST-selected AGN up to zâ=â11. Orange squares show recently identified Euclid quasars, and the green star shows DÃºn Aonghasa, which is more UV-luminous than the LRDs, other JWST-selected AGN, and Lyman-break galaxies at comparable redshifts. JWST-selected AGN are shown as circles and colour-coded according to their phenomenological classification: LRDs in red, LBDs in blue, and other AGN in black. Previously known quasars are shown as grey circles. Open purple diamonds are Lyman-break galaxies. Image Credit: J. Wolf et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A356

DÃºn Aonghasa and its high redshift brethren pose the same familiar question: how did they get so large so quickly?

"Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth," the authors write.

While an actual answer to their growth is elusive, finding them helps constrain an eventual answer.

âFinding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew,â said lead author Wolf in a press release. âThe closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth â or both.â

Aside from their puzzling masses, these quasars also open different windows or probes into aspects of the early Universe. They give astronomers long sightlines into the intergalactic medium, letting them study its opacity during reionization, and its metal enrichment.

The quasars also serve as probes of how matter was distributed. "Quasars further mark rare, highly biased peaks in the underlying matter distribution and therefore trace the densest regions of the early large-scale structure," the researchers write.

On galactic scales, these high-redshift quasars are probes of how SMBH masses and the masses of their host galaxies co-evolved. Both masses tend to correlate, but there's no obvious reason why. AGN feedback could play a role, so could mergers, or a shared source of fuel for growth. But there's no certainty, so finding more high-redshift quasars may lead to an answer.

These things are all related, but the main result of finding these quasars is facing the questions posed by their high masses.

Finding these quasars and supermassive black holes is forcing astronomers to consider different explanations for how they grew so massive so quickly. One explanation is super-Eddington accretion, but DÃºn Aonghasa isn't accreting matter that rapidly. Another is massive seeds, but current formation models struggle to accommodate those. Another explanation is that quasars experienced super-Eddington accretion very early in the Universe, under very different conditions.

Heavy seeds could explain these quasars, but what could they be? Astrophysicists don't know, but some candidates are Direct-Collapse Black Holes, or maybe sequential runaway stellar collisions in extremely dense star clusters.

Another, more exotic and theoretical possibility for heavy seeds is primordial black holes (PBH). These are theorized to have formed in the very first moments in the Universe, when dense pockets of gas collapsed directly into black holes. With such an early head start, these PBH could've formed into heavy seeds without needing physics-breaking levels of accretion.

Primordial black holes are only hypothetical. If they're real, they could've formed by direct collapse of dense pockets of matter shortly after the Big Bang. They could've acted as seeds for the very early, very massive SMBH found in the Epoch of Reionization. Image Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann., CC BY-SA

Luminous quasars like DÃºn Aonghasa are rare in the Epoch of Reionization. So far, there are only seven of them. The only path to an explanation for their masses is through more observations that find more of these ancient quasars, and hopefully ones even more distant.

âAnd this may happen sooner than we think,â said co-author Silvia Belladitta a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy. âThis highlights how quickly Euclid is expanding our census of the most distant quasars. Each new discovery brings us closer to understanding how supermassive black holes formed and grew in the early universe.â

"DÃºn Aonghasa establishes a new quasar redshift frontier as the first confirmed quasar at zâ>â8, providing a powerful new benchmark for early SMBH growth," the researchers write in their paper's conclusion. Its large mass shows that it must have grown a lot before it was observed, but its bolometric luminosity contradicts that. So the mystery of massive early SMBH and their quasars is still a puzzle.

Researchers predicted that Euclid will find between 8â23 quasars at zâ>â8, so hopefully, more are on their way.

âIt is unclear how far back in time these supermassive black holes powering luminous quasars exist, but Euclid has a good chance of finding out what that limit is,â said MPIA scientist and co-author Eduardo BaÃ±ados.

It might seem like researchers are chasing a receding horizon, almost like a dog chasing its tail. They build better telescopes in hopes of finding answers to difficult questions. Then their telescopes uncover some answers, but also uncover more questions. It's probably true that there's no end to knowledge and we'll never know everything. But that also means there's no end to learning, no end to Nature, and no end to wonder.

#6404. Scientists Discover 130-Year-Old Fish Still Swimming in an American River

Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

The findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

The blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

“For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”

To investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of new generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

The researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann said.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann said. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

“This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

The blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Blue suckers also challenge expectations about how river environments shape animal lifespans. Unlike fish inhabiting relatively calm lakes, they spend their lives in fast-flowing rivers, where maintaining position and navigating currents can require considerable energy. Such environments have often been associated with faster life histories, making the species’ extreme longevity particularly unexpected.

The oldest fish examined had already been alive for decades when many of the dams now shaping the Missouri River system were constructed. Their survival across more than a century of environmental change contrasts with the apparent scarcity of younger generations, raising conservation concerns about whether aging adults are being replaced.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” said Holmquist.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”

Reference: “Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA” by Alec R. Lackmann, Allen H. Andrews, Luke M. Holmquist, Negar Haghipour, Grant Grisak, Molly A. H. Webb, Mark E. Clark and Zachary R. Shattuck, 18 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3

Funding for this project was provided by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks and NorthWestern Energy. The study was also coauthored by Negar Haghipour (ETH Zürich), Grant Grisak (NorthWestern Energy), Molly Webb (USFWS), Mark Clark (UMD – Biology), and Zach Shattuck (MTFWP).
