#6387. Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

“AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”

The first light of dawn illuminates a sea of fog spilling over the rugged cliffs of Mallorca, Spain, in this year's winning Weather Photographer of the Year 2026 image. Photographer Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the scene from the Albercutz Watchtower, looking toward the Formentor Peninsula, after several days of high pressure and humid nights created the perfect conditions for fog to blanket the landscape.

On Nov. 17, the photograph, titled "Mares de Niebla (Seas of Fog)," was named overall winner of the Royal Meteorological Society's competition, which attracted more than 5,500 entries from photographers around the world.

The competition celebrates the ephemeral scenes created by weather, which can for brief moments transform landscapes into something extraordinary. Take a look at this year's winning photographs below and let us know your favorites in the comments.

Photographer Weilu Chen took second place in the main category with this spectacular image of golden light shining over the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge that runs for 34 miles (55 kilometers) across the Pearl River estuary in southern China.

A striking bolt of lightning illuminates a horizontal cloud during a thunderstorm, earning third place in the main category. These clouds are called arcus clouds that have a distinct shelf-like shape. "Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night," photographer Laura Hedien said in a statement.

Photographer Mahmudul Hasan won first place in the public vote category for this image of the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.

Watching from Bayonne, New Jersey, photographer Dan Martland captured this triple lightning strike above New York City, earning second place in the public vote category.

#6384. An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward new ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

The system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

“This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” says Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

“Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker says. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

“Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”

#6383. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6382. Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer New Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering new clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer new clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham said, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study shows just how much has been hidden.”

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others showed the opposite pattern.

Dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”

Studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

The researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

Such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

In the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, said, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”

Future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

Dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”

“Population-level characterization of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites” by Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, Francesco Asnicar, Daniel Kirk, Ricardo Costeira, Nicola Segata, Mario Falchi, Jordana T. Bell, Tim D. Spector, Lindsey A. Edwards, Li Deng, Ana M. Valdes and Cristina Menni, 17 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79230-0

“Large-scale shotgun metagenomic analysis of gut bacteria–phage interactions in IBS” by Daniel Kirk, Erfan Khamespanah, Panayiotis Louca, Alessia Visconti, Robert Pope, Francesco Asnicar, Sarah E Berry, Jonathan Wolf, Nicola Segata, Tim D Spector, Mario Falchi, Frances M K Williams, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Li Deng and Cristina Menni, 16 November 2026, Gut. DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2026-338807

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

#6380. Semiconductor Breakthrough Cracks a Longstanding Solar Energy Problem

An unusual material could help us make better use of the sun’s energy, offering new possibilities for more efficient solar power and fuel production.

Generating more electricity from sunlight does not necessarily mean installing more solar panels. Finding ways to extract more energy from the light that already reaches them could make solar power a more practical source of electricity. Part of the challenge lies in what happens inside a solar cell in the moments after it absorbs sunlight.

Solar cells contain materials called semiconductors, which use the energy from sunlight to free negatively charged electrons, leaving behind positively charged gaps known as holes. Both charges must be collected to generate electricity. If an electron and a hole meet and cancel each other out, a process known as recombination, the energy they carry is lost. Unfortunately, materials that are particularly good at absorbing sunlight also tend to lose these charges more quickly.

A study led by the University of Oxford has identified a promising exception in a semiconductor called bismuth sulfide. Published October 28, 2026, in Nature, the research examined how the material’s unusual electronic structure could help overcome this longstanding limitation in solar energy technology.

To investigate how long electrical charges survive in bismuth sulfide, the researchers exposed thin films of the material to extremely short laser pulses. They then tracked how quickly the charges disappeared using a technique called ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, conducting measurements at temperatures ranging from room temperature to just above absolute zero.

“One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly,” said corresponding author Professor Laura Herz (Department of Physics, University of Oxford). “Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable. By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently.”

Electronic structure calculations by Professor Marina Filip’s group in Oxford’s Department of Physics helped explain why bismuth sulfide behaves differently. The material has two closely spaced routes through which electrons can move between energy levels. One allows the material to absorb light strongly, while the other sits at a slightly lower energy and allows charges to disappear much more slowly. Because the two are so close together, charges spend much of their time in the lower-energy states, which effectively serve as a temporary storage reservoir.

Cooling the material provided further evidence for this explanation. In most semiconductors, electrical charges disappear faster as temperatures drop. In bismuth sulfide, more charges settled into the reservoir as the material cooled, allowing them to survive longer. The results matched the team’s model of what physicists call a pseudo-direct semiconductor.

Even at room temperature, the researchers estimate that this arrangement reduces the rate of charge loss by about 75% compared with conventional semiconductors that absorb light equally well.

Giving electrical charges more time to be collected could improve the efficiency of solar panels without compromising their ability to capture sunlight. The benefits could also extend beyond electricity generation. Longer-lived charges could provide more time for the chemical reactions needed to produce fuels using sunlight.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”

The team’s calculations suggest that researchers could search existing materials databases for semiconductors with similar properties or engineer new ones. However, the study demonstrates the underlying physical mechanism rather than the performance of a finished solar cell. Further research will be needed to determine how these properties can be put to use in solar energy technologies.

Reference: “Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor” by Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip and Laura M. Herz, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6376. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

Black Friday sales are live for tons of top items, including power tools, hand tools, larger appliances, and more at Lowe’s and Home Depot. That said, between the two established hardware stores, which one is offering better deals?

The answer is complicated and boils down to a few key questions: What exactly are you looking for, and how much do you need? While both offer discounted power tools, Home Depot offers its biggest savings when you buy multiple items. Lowe's, on the other hand, focuses more on traditional discounts on single tools. Take a look at some of the sales we highlight below.

Before you read on, it’s important to clarify that both retailers offer bundle deals, straight discounts, and buy-one-get-one offers. In fact, they even have a few sales that are quite similar to one another like the DeWalt cordless 20-volt drill at both Lowe’s and Home Depot.

However, a lot of the best deals we saw at Lowe’s were simple discounts while Home Depot had a lot more based on getting additional tools free with purchase.

We typically lean toward Lowe’s over Home Depot because that simplicity tends to leave more money in your wallet. If all you’re buying is one drill, you can get it on sale at Lowe’s without needing to buy a single additional item to maximize the savings. While you might not save the same percentage compared to the retail price, you’ll spend fewer total dollars, which, to us, feels like the true bottom line.

For instance, this Craftsman nailer that is $60 off comes with no charger or battery. If you already own Craftsman power tools, this is no problem at all. In fact, it lowers the total price of your purchase.

Similarly, the Craftsman steel tool chest, which is being discounted $120 doesn’t come with additional hand tools or accessories. Just a plain old tool chest at a massive discount.

If you want to reset your tool selection, Home Depot offers deals on larger bundles. Many of its best Black Friday sales aren’t standalone discounts; they’re built around add-ons. If you buy one combo kit, you can get an additional power tool from the brand for free.

A great example of this is the Milwaukee combo kit. It includes a Packout rolling toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger. On top of the 42 percent discount, the kit includes a “free” 18-volt battery pack that typically retails for around 230 bucks. This further adds to the savings, but it comes with the caveat of making a large, multi-tool purchase.

Shopping at either Lowe’s or Home Depot during Black Friday will get you a ton of good deals. You can’t make a serious mistake either way. However, we lean a little more toward Lowe’s because it's often cheaper overall if you only want a few specific items. The best savings will come from buying only what you need instead of chasing the biggest discounts. Lowe’s offers the best chance to leave without feeling like you got a few fluff pieces you didn’t really need.

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

STEM-based schoolwork is a key part of your kid’s curriculum, but encouraging genuine enthusiasm for science, technology, engineering, and math that extends beyond the classroom requires more than a good teacher. For the right kid at the right age, a robotics kit may be a perfect fit. It can give a budding inventor the chance to learn about science in a practical way, on their own terms, and allows them to get creative. Not all of them do that effectively, though: Choosing the right one for the child in your life may not be so straightforward—particularly if you’re unfamiliar with the basics that robotics kits teach. To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. Whether you're getting ahead of shopping season or looking for a great last-minute holiday gift, these toys are both fun and give your child's mind a chance to grow.

During our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

To make our selections, we looked for kits from reputable companies within the robotics space, such as Learning Resources and Wonder Workshop. We also took a look at toys and items that parents on the staff have bought for their own kids, making special note of any that ended up as household favorites.

While evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

If you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of new ways to play.

The robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a new toy.

A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

You can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

Once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

This 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

For parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their new skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

This coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

Makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

The robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

There’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. It’s reasonably priced for what it offers, has a super-cool LED matrix that shows off characters and vector graphics, and boasts a top speed of 4.5 mph. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

What makes this robot special is how it allows users to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

Robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

The finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

One of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

This kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

Protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

Studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

Choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the company or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

You don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse.

The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment.

The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells.

"This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow, an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons.

The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals. Known as "SwAP-In," it enables researchers to rewrite large portions of an organism's genetic code by inserting big chunks of synthetic DNA. In this case, the approach was used to insert a human gene into lab mice.

"It is kind of a generic method that can be used to make extensively humanized mice," said study co-author Jef Boeke, director of the Institute for Systems Genetics at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a lead developer of the SwAP-In technique.

Liddelow anticipates that this new method for humanizing mice, or tweaking their biology to more closely match that of humans, will prove useful for studying a wide range of diseases, from common conditions like Alzheimer's to "orphan" diseases like XDP, which are rare, underresearched and lacking effective treatments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

XDP is a neurodegenerative condition that particularly impacts the striatum, part of the brain that's crucial for movement. The disease causes symptoms such as slowed movements, tremors, muscle stiffness and involuntary muscle contractions.

On average, symptoms emerge around age 39 and patients live for 13 to 16 years after their symptoms appear. In late stages of the disease, problems with breathing and swallowing can lead to deadly complications such as malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Historically, XDP has also carried a lot of social stigma, which has contributed to high rates of depression and suicide among those with the condition.

"Patients get sort of shunned and hidden away," Liddelow said. That, among other factors, made XDP difficult to study.

XDP shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (depicted above).

Although XDP isn't fully understood, its underlying genetic cause is known. It stems from a mutation in TAF1, a gene on the X chromosome that helps translate DNA sequences into new proteins. Because males carry only one X chromosome — and thus have no backup copy of the gene — the condition affects far more males than females.

The mutation first appeared in a person on Panay, an island in the Philippines. Due to a phenomenon called the "founder effect," it has risen in prevalence among people of Filipino ancestry but is not seen in other demographics, Boeke explained. Studies suggest there are about 5.7 cases per 100,000 people in the Philippines.

XDP's rarity and associated stigma have made the condition difficult to study, but there's another layer of complexity: The mutation in TAF1 was originally caused by a "jumping gene" ‪—‬ a bit of DNA that changed its position within the genome. In this instance, the DNA happened to jump into the middle of TAF1 and disrupted its function, Boeke said.

But the jumping gene in question is found only in primates. Ideally, if you wanted to study the disease in lab mice, you'd have to insert that jumping gene into their DNA — and that's exactly what the researchers did in the first of their two new studies.

Using SwAP-In, the team inserted 78,000 "letters" of human DNA code into mouse embryonic stem cells. This code included part of the human version of the TAF1 gene and the relevant jumping gene that causes XDP. In both lab dishes and living mice, this gene insertion triggered the telltale signs of XDP: low levels of the TAF1 protein, cell death and holes in the brain, especially in the striatum.

One big difference between mice and humans is that the mouse version of XDP progresses very quickly, with symptoms appearing in just 1.5 months, whereas the human disease takes years to show up. That may be because human bodies have safeguards to help offset the jumping gene's effects — at least for a while — while mice lack this safety net, the study authors theorized.

That difference in disease progression is actually a "huge advantage" for researchers, Boeke noted. "Because it's so sped up, it's possible to do experiments on therapeutics," he said. For instance, if an experimental drug is successfully fighting the disease, that should be obvious in the mice, whose condition would otherwise progress very quickly.

I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients.

In the second of the team's new studies, they took a closer look at the new mice with XDP, to see how the disorder affected their brain cells. Through a battery of tests, they realized that glial cells known as oligodendrocytes showed dramatic changes in both their overall numbers and their gene activity.

These cells would normally make a fatty insulating material called myelin, which wraps around the outgoing wires of neurons to help them send signals. To see how the cells were faring in the XDP mice, study co-author Priya Prakash, a postdoctoral scholar in Liddelow's lab, used a blue stain to label the cells within the mouse brain tissue.

"Where you would normally see this beautiful blue brain, full of lipid, full of myelin, you essentially see a white brain, with none of this lipid there," Liddelow said. This was especially apparent in the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

Further experiments revealed that the mutation was preventing oligodendrocytes from fully maturing, and that reduced the amount of myelin made in these parts of the brain. They backed up these findings in brains of people with XDP that had been donated after death.

The researchers think this extensive loss of insulation may leave neurons vulnerable to dying early, Liddelow said. In short, "this is a neurodegenerative disease that may not first be manifesting in neurons themselves," he emphasized. "I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients."

Together, the studies raise several ideas for treating XDP. One treatment could involve cranking up the activity of the TAF1 gene to boost the levels of its related protein. This idea showed promise in experiments with mouse cells in the team's first paper. The second paper points to oligodendrocytes as potential targets for future therapies, and myelin loss as a potential early sign of the disease that might be useful for diagnosis.

There's still much more to learn about the biology of XDP and what types of treatments might reverse the drivers of the disease, Liddelow and Boeke emphasized. But now, other scientists have access to a brand-new mouse model that can help them solve the disease's remaining mysteries.

#6367. At the Races: Regional realignment

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6364. Save Over $1,100 on Sony’s Already Budget-Friendly Bravia 3 II During Black Friday

The editor-tested unit is now nearly 40% off.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

We’re huge fans of Sony TVs here at Pop Mech, but there is an elephant in the room—they’re pretty damn expensive. While it’s sometimes hard to recommend some of its high-end models to our readers (at least from a sticker-shock perspective), Sony does make a budget-friendly option at a far more accessible price point: the Sony BRAVIA 3 II.

Better news: During Black Friday, you can save over $1,100 on the editor-tested 4K TV for a limited time. And it’s available on Amazon.

The $1,100 in savings applies to the 100-inch Bravia 3 II, but a few sizes are on sale. You can save over $100 on the 55-inch (now $698) and the 65-inch (now $798). As you move up in size, the savings multiply. The 75-inch version is over $200 off, and the 85-inch unit is more than $400 off. The 100-inch version is the big kahuna, but there are plenty of savings to go around.

The Bravia 3 II is Sony’s mid-tier, wallet-friendly option, but keep in mind that the BRAVIA line is high-end, so it’s essentially a mid-tier “plus.” In essence, it offers a cinema-like experience at an accessible price point. The device’s proprietary X-Balanced Speakers deliver deeper bass and clearer sound resolution, and it supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, plus integrated DTS:X surround sound for an immersive, theater-like experience.

While it’s ideal for movie buffs, it also features an enhanced 120Hz refresh rate for sports and live TV.
